noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to apply the rules of International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature to: i name compounds relevant to this specification ii draw these compounds, as they are encountered in the specification, using structural, displayed and skeletal formulae Students will be expected to know prefixes for compounds up to C 10
be able to classify reactions as addition, substitution, oxidation, reduction or polymerisation

primer.text: Every organic name is constructive: an alkane stem counts the longest chain, locants minimise from the nearest end, alkyl branches take -yl and di-, tri-, tetra- prefixes, and functional groups claim their endings. Reactions then classify into addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis and condensation, with organic redox reading oxygen in and hydrogen out. This note drills names and reaction families.

lessons.title: Stems, chains and the lowest numbers
lessons.opening: Systematic nomenclature gives every organic compound one unambiguous name, built on the alkane stems: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent- and onward count the carbons in the longest chain. Side-chains enter in brackets as alkyl groups, their positions numbered from whichever chain end gives the lowest numbers, with di-, tri-, tetra- for repeats, commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and words.
keyPoints: Systematic nomenclature names organic compounds so they are easy to refer to unambiguously.
Alkane stems encode the carbon count of the longest chain: meth- (1) through dec- (10).
Positions are numbered from the chain end that gives the lowest possible numbers.
Side-chains appear in brackets as alkyl groups, named by adding -yl to the alkane stem.
Repeats take di-, tri- or tetra-; different side-chains list alphabetically; commas join adjacent numbers, hyphens join numbers to words.

low.restatement: Count the longest chain for the stem, number from the end that keeps the numbers small, and bracket any branches as -yl groups.
low.analogy: House numbering on a street: the block length names the street, and doors are numbered from whichever end keeps addresses lowest.
low.examPointer: The lowest-number rule is the most-tested convention - if your name has a higher locant than it needs, it is wrong.

medium.restatement: The grammar of IUPAC names decomposes into stem (chain length), locants (position numbers, minimised), prefixes (di/tri/tetra multiplicity, alphabetical listing of different substituents) and suffixes (functional-group endings), with punctuation rules: commas between adjacent numbers, hyphens between numbers and letters.
medium.analogy: A postal address grammar: street (stem), door numbers (locants), flat labels (prefixes), all punctuated by fixed conventions.
medium.examPointer: Alphabetise by side-chain name, ignoring the di-/tri- prefixes - ethyl sorts before dimethyl in a name listing both.

check.stem: In systematic nomenclature, what does the stem of an IUPAC name encode?

options.text: The number of carbon atoms in the longest chain
options.explanation: Meth- through dec- count one to ten.
Suffixes and infixes carry the functional group.
Mass is not encoded in the stem.

check.stem: Which stem corresponds to a four-carbon longest chain?
How are the carbon atoms of the longest chain numbered when naming?

options.text: From whichever chain end keeps the side-chain numbers lowest
Always from the left as drawn
options.explanation: Drawing orientation is arbitrary; the rule is about lowest locants.

options.text: From the end nearest the functional group only
options.explanation: The general rule is lowest numbers overall.

options.text: From either end - both give valid names
options.explanation: Only the lowest-locant name is correct.

check.stem: How is a hydrocarbon side-chain named?

options.text: Take the alkane stem, append -yl, and bracket it in the formula
By counting it as a separate molecule
options.explanation: Side-chains are part of the one molecule.

check.stem: Two methyl groups appear on the same chain. How is this encoded in the name?

options.text: As dimethyl, with a comma between adjacent position numbers
options.explanation: di- marks two, commas join the numbers.

options.text: As methyl methyl with a space

options.explanation: bi- is not the organic prefix.

check.stem: State the alkane stems for chains of one to five carbons.
check.modelAnswer: Meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent- count one through five carbons.

check.stem: State the punctuation rules connecting numbers and words in organic names.
check.modelAnswer: Adjacent numbers take a comma between them; numbers separate from words by a hyphen.

check.stem: Explain why the lowest-number rule exists in systematic nomenclature.
check.modelAnswer: A branched chain can be numbered from either end, giving different locants for the same molecule; fixing on the lowest set makes the name unique, which is the entire purpose of systematic nomenclature.

check.stem: Name CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 systematically, showing the stem and locant reasoning.
check.modelAnswer: The longest chain carries four carbons (but-); numbering from the nearer end puts the methyl branch on carbon 2; the name is 2-methylbutane.

lessons.title: Functional groups claim the names
lessons.opening: Functional groups stamp their identity onto the name: the nomenclature table pairs each family - alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines, nitriles - with the ending or infix that announces it. Read the table's pattern and any structure converts into its systematic name.
keyPoints: The nomenclature table summarises examples, nomenclature and names for each functional-group family.
The families covered include alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amines and nitriles.
Each family's ending or infix is the naming signal for its functional group.
Naming a molecule means combining the alkane stem, the locants and the family's naming signal.
The systematic name pins down both the carbon skeleton and the functional group.

low.restatement: Every functional family owns a piece of the name: find the group in the table, borrow its ending, and attach it to the chain stem.
low.analogy: Football kit numbers: the squad (stem) stays fixed, but the number (ending) announces the player's role.
low.examPointer: Practise reading the table in both directions - structure to name and name to structure.

medium.restatement: The nomenclature table is the decoder ring of organic names: each functional group maps to a fixed naming signal which compounds with the stem and locant machinery, so the full name encodes skeleton and function simultaneously.
medium.analogy: A license-plate code: region letters (stem), serial numbers (locants) and class badge (functional ending) jointly identify the vehicle.
medium.examPointer: Do not mix up family endings - alcohols and aldehydes sound alike but name different groups.

check.stem: What does the functional-group nomenclature table provide?

options.text: Examples, nomenclature and names for each functional-group family

options.explanation: Physical data is not the table's job.
Mechanisms are not in the naming table.

check.stem: Which set of families appears in the nomenclature table?

options.text: From alkenes through alcohols, aldehydes and ketones to acids, esters, amines and nitriles
options.explanation: The eight families of the table of record.
The table reaches far beyond hydrocarbons.

check.stem: What must a systematic name combine to be complete?

options.text: The alkane stem, the locants and the functional group's naming signal
options.explanation: All three encode the structure fully.
Mass is not part of the name.

check.stem: A name ending announced by the table tells you

options.text: which functional group the molecule carries

check.stem: Reading the table backwards - from a systematic name to a structure - is possible because

options.text: each part of the name encodes one structural feature
options.explanation: Stem, locants and signal rebuild the molecule.

options.text: the table lists every possible molecule
options.explanation: The rules generalise beyond the table's examples.

check.stem: Name the eight functional-group families in the nomenclature table.
check.modelAnswer: Alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines and nitriles.

check.stem: State the three structural features a complete systematic name encodes.
check.modelAnswer: The carbon skeleton (stem), the positions (locants) and the functional group (the family's naming signal).

check.stem: Explain why systematic names are preferable to trivial names for organic compounds.
check.modelAnswer: Millions of organic structures exist, far beyond memory; a constructive naming system lets any chemist decode the structure from the name - and build the name from any structure - without a lookup table of trivia.

check.stem: A structure carries a four-carbon chain with an -OH on carbon 2. Assemble its systematic name from stem, locant and family signal.
check.modelAnswer: Stem but- (four carbons), locant 2, alcohol signal: butan-2-ol.

lessons.title: Five reaction families
lessons.opening: Organic reactions sort into five named types. Addition joins two or more molecules into a single product and nothing else; substitution swaps one atom or group for another; elimination ejects a small molecule like water or HCl; hydrolysis splits a compound with water; condensation joins two molecules while eliminating a small molecule as a by-product.
keyPoints: An addition reaction combines two or more molecules into a single product with no other products.
A substitution reaction replaces an atom or group of atoms with another.
An elimination reaction removes a small molecule such as H2O or HCl from the organic molecule.
A hydrolysis reaction breaks a compound down by water (or dilute acid or alkali).
A condensation reaction joins two organic molecules and eliminates a small molecule such as H2O or HCl.

low.restatement: Addition merges, substitution swaps, elimination ejects, hydrolysis splits with water, condensation joins-and-ejects.
low.analogy: Five kinds of LEGO move: snap two bricks into one, pop a stud out for another, flick a tiny brick off, soak a joint apart, or snap two bricks together while flicking a bit off.
low.examPointer: Addition and condensation are mirror opposites on product count: one product versus products-plus-small-molecule.

medium.restatement: The classification tracks atom economy and by-products: addition is fully incorporating, substitution exchanges, elimination exports a small molecule, hydrolysis imports water to cleave, and condensation couples an addition with an elimination - water or HCl leaving as the joint is made.
medium.analogy: Five warehouse operations: full intake, swap-in-swap-out, export, delivery-assisted dismantling, and a combined intake-plus-export shipment.
medium.examPointer: Name the small molecule when classifying eliminations and condensations - H2O or HCl - the specificity is the mark.

check.stem: Which reaction type forms a single product from two or more molecules?
Swapping one atom or atom-group out for another defines which reaction type?

options.explanation: One group swaps out for another.

check.stem: Which small molecules does the note name as typical elimination products?

options.explanation: Water or hydrogen chloride leave the organic molecule.
Neither appears in the elimination definition.
Combustion products, not the named small molecules.

check.stem: What agent breaks down a compound in hydrolysis?

options.text: Water - or dilute acids or alkali as the broader usage

check.stem: How does condensation differ from addition?

options.text: Condensation joins two molecules AND eliminates a small molecule; addition gives only the single product

check.stem: Define an addition reaction.
check.modelAnswer: In an addition reaction, two or more molecules merge into one product - and nothing else forms alongside it.

check.stem: Define a condensation reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A condensation reaction joins two organic molecules together while eliminating a small molecule such as H2O or HCl.

check.stem: Explain why hydrolysis can be described as the opposite of condensation.
check.modelAnswer: Condensation joins two molecules while exporting water; hydrolysis imports water to break a compound apart - the same water appears as by-product in one and reagent in the other.

check.stem: Classify each: ethene absorbing HBr into one product; ethanol losing water to an alkene; an ester splitting with water.
check.modelAnswer: Addition (single product formed), elimination (water removed), hydrolysis (water splits the ester).

lessons.title: Redox shorthand and polymer chains
lessons.opening: Organic redox counts oxygens and hydrogens: oxidation adds oxygen or removes hydrogen atoms - or removes electrons or raises the oxidation number - and reduction runs reverse. Equation shorthand writes [O] for the oxidising agent's oxygen atom and [H] for the reducing agent's hydrogen atom. At AS level, polymerisation means addition polymerisation: many C=C-bearing monomers chain into the polymer as the only product.
keyPoints: Oxidation adds oxygen, removes electrons or increases the oxidation number - in organic work, adding O or removing H atoms.
Reduction removes oxygen, adds electrons or decreases the oxidation number - in organic work, removing O or adding H atoms.
[O] represents one oxygen atom from an oxidising agent in organic equations; [H] represents one hydrogen atom from a reducing agent.
All AS-level polymerisation covered is addition polymerisation.
Addition polymerisation takes many C=C-bearing monomers and chains them into polymer as the sole product.

low.restatement: Organic oxidation = more oxygen or fewer hydrogens; reduction = fewer oxygens or more hydrogens. [O] and [H] are the shorthand guests in equations. Monomers with C=C chain up into polymers alone.
low.analogy: A see-saw of O and H tokens: loading oxygen tips toward oxidation, loading hydrogen tips back toward reduction.
low.examPointer: The [O]/[H] symbols represent atoms from the agent, not the agent itself - phrase answers carefully.

medium.restatement: Organic redox reinterprets the general electron bookkeeping in structural terms - oxygen in or hydrogen out raises the oxidation state of carbon; the reverse lowers it. Addition polymerisation then exploits the C=C bond: opening the double bond across many monomers incorporates everything into one saturated chain with no by-products.
medium.analogy: Rungs of a ladder join end to end: every double-bond rung consumed becomes part of one continuous rail - nothing left over.
medium.examPointer: 'As the only product' is the addition-polymerisation phrase to quote - condensation polymerisation does not appear at AS here.

check.stem: In organic chemistry, oxidation often means

options.text: adding oxygen atoms or removing hydrogen atoms

check.stem: What does [O] represent in an organic redox equation?

options.text: A single oxygen atom donated by the oxidising agent
A whole molecule of oxygen gas

options.explanation: Only its oxygen atom is represented.

check.stem: A substance gains hydrogen atoms. What has happened to it?

options.explanation: Hydrogen gain is the organic reduction signature.
Hydrogen loss, not gain, is oxidation.

check.stem: Which monomers undergo addition polymerisation?

options.text: Molecules carrying a C=C double bond somewhere in them
options.explanation: The double bond is the polymerisation handle.
Single bonds cannot open to chain.

check.stem: What, besides the polymer, do addition polymerisation reactions produce?

options.text: Nothing - the polymer is the only product

options.explanation: The monomers are consumed into the polymer.

check.stem: State the three general definitions of oxidation.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen joins the substance, electrons leave it, or its oxidation number climbs.

check.stem: State the [H] shorthand's meaning and the monomer requirement for addition polymerisation.
check.modelAnswer: [H] represents one hydrogen atom from a reducing agent; monomers must carry at least one C-C double bond.

check.stem: Explain why addition polymerisation leaves no by-products.
check.modelAnswer: The C=C double bonds of every monomer open and link directly into the chain, so every atom of every monomer ends up inside the polymer - unlike condensation, no small molecule is ejected.

check.stem: Write the organic-redox direction when an alcohol becomes an aldehyde, using the [O] shorthand, and classify the change.
check.modelAnswer: Alcohol plus [O] gives aldehyde plus water: oxygen is added (and hydrogens effectively removed), so the alcohol is oxidised.

glossary.definition: A hydrocarbon side-chain named by adding -yl to the alkane stem, shown in brackets in the structural formula.
A reaction replacing an atom or group of atoms with another.
The reaction chaining many C=C-bearing monomers into a polymer as the only product.
A reaction joining two organic molecules while eliminating a small molecule such as H2O or HCl.

steps: Find the longest chain: four carbons, giving the stem but-.
Number from the end nearer the branch so the locant is lowest: the methyl group sits on carbon 2.
Combine stem, locant and alkyl prefix: 2-methylbutane.
